title: New Toll After Nepal Floods: 600+ Dead, 3K Missing - Newser
description: New Toll After Nepal Floods: 600+ Dead, 3K Missing  Newser
publisher.title: Newser
full_article:
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. In Nuwakot, one of Nepal's districts devastated by the floods, helicopters resumed operations before noon on Saturday after poor weather temporarily hampered aerial rescue activities. Some helicopters were loaded with boxes and bags of aid, including clothes, instant noodles, crackers, and rice; others returned from the flood-hit areas carrying survivors. The evacuees had been brought from the nearby community of Trishuli. As people were still leaving Trishuli, however, some residents were returning to see what could be salvaged from their decimated homes. One boy walked out of the village carrying muddy sandals from his house.

Another woman who returned found her dog, Sweetie, whom she was forced to leave behind when the floods came. She sat on the ground petting her dog and feeding her water from a bottle. In Kathmandu, Nepal's capital, relatives and friends gathered outside the main government hospital starting in the early morning, desperately searching for news of missing loved ones. Many shuffled between the help desk and the hospital notice board, clutching photos and scanning lists of injured patients.

Search and rescue efforts continued at several locations in Nepal and China's Tibet, including the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Nepal's Rasuwa district and the severely damaged Gyirong border crossing on the Chinese side. A rep for Nepal's army, Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, said rescue efforts would continue at the hydropower construction site, where authorities believe more than 100 people are trapped in a tunnel filled with thick mud. He said rescue teams had also been forced to relocate temporarily when authorities issued warnings about possible further flooding. More here.

When they fast melt, then mountains destabilise and we see increased incidents of rockfalls, landslides, avalanches and debris floods – as we are seeing in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region. Because of warming, experts say, higher parts of mountains now also see rains instead of snow that can also make them unstable. Environment correspondent, BBC World Service How much of a role climate change played in the collapse of the glacier that caused this devastating flood might be known if there are focused studies in the days to come. But what we already know is that global warming has led to accelerated melting of Himalayas' glaciers, icefields, snowpacks and permafrost. Scientists say thinning and retreating of glaciers can not only cause their collapse but can also rapidly fill up glacial lakes that can then burst out causing floods. They say ice and snow buttress mountain slopes – just like cement keeps buildings intact. When they fast melt, then mountains destabilise and we see increased incidents of rockfalls, landslides, avalanches and debris floods – as we are seeing in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region. Because of warming, experts say, higher parts of mountains now also see rains instead of snow that can also make them unstable. A study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development released in March showed that ice loss rates in the region have doubled since 2000. full_article:
The scale of destruction along Nepal’s northern frontier is coming into sharper focus after flooding and mudslides tore through the area, killing hundreds of people and leaving thousands of others unaccounted for.

Death toll nears 700 in catastrophic Nepal-China floods amid search efforts (Video: CNN Newsource)

After Nepali authorities updated their figures on Saturday, the combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 676 dead and nearly 3,000 people missing. Chinese authorities have reported seven deaths and more than 550 missing, while Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 669 with 2,426 people missing.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far.

NUWAKOT, NEPAL - AUGUST 28: An Aerial view shows debris and mud covering an area following flash floods on August 28, 2026 in DevGhat village, Nepal. Authorities said the flash floods were triggered after a mass of ice, mud and rock collapsed into a Himalayan river near the Nepal-China border, leaving hundreds dead or missing and causing widespread damage in affected districts. Authorities continued the gruelling search for victims, many buried under metres of mud, as both China and Nepal issued fresh flooding alerts. (Photo by Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images)

The disaster hit near Nepal’s border with China earlier this week, with fast-moving water and debris ripping through settlements, damaging roads and bridges, and cutting off access to areas normally reached only by narrow mountain routes.

Search teams have been working through mud, wreckage, and unstable terrain to find survivors and recover victims. The conditions have slowed the effort, forcing rescuers to rely on helicopters and other air support to reach communities separated by washed-out roads.

NUWAKOT, NEPAL - AUGUST 28: An aerial view shows A collapsed bridge following flash floods on August 28, 2026 in DeviGhat village, Nepal. Authorities said the flash floods were triggered after a mass of ice, mud and rock collapsed into a Himalayan river near the Nepal-China border, leaving hundreds dead or missing and causing widespread damage in affected districts. Authorities continued the gruelling search for victims, many buried under metres of mud, as both China and Nepal issued fresh flooding alerts. (Photo by Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images)

Officials said the missing include local residents, workers, and foreign visitors traveling through the region, including Americans. About 90 Americans are among those unaccounted for, according to the U.S. State Department.

Families have gathered at relief sites and hospitals seeking information about relatives swept away or stranded by the flooding.

The emergency has also damaged infrastructure needed for longer-term recovery, including transportation links and hydropower facilities. Authorities face the added challenge of assessing conditions in high-altitude areas where landslides and further flooding remain possible.

The disaster has prompted Nepal to seek outside assistance as crews continue rescue and recovery operations. Chinese authorities also reported deaths and missing people in Tibet, across the border.

title: When a mountain falls: How ice and rock triggered Nepal’s catastrophic flood – and why climate change is raising the risks - The Conversation
description: When a mountain falls: How ice and rock triggered Nepal’s catastrophic flood – and why climate change is raising the risks  The Conversation
publisher.title: The Conversation
full_article:
The catastrophic flood that killed hundreds of people in Nepal on Aug. 26, 2026, and left many more missing likely began with falling ice and rock crashing into the river below, but that wasn’t the end of the disaster. Days later, a new lake pooled behind the debris and then burst, sending more water streaming through the valley.

The destruction represents two of the ways rising temperatures, thawing permafrost and melting ice are increasing the risk of destructive floods in the Himalayas and other high mountain regions around the world.

I am a geologist and part of an ad hoc international group of 50-plus scientists who meet quickly after mountain disasters to analyze satellite images and field data to get information out to the public. This is what we’ve learned so far about the disaster and the region’s rising risks from climate change.

The flood disaster in Nepal

Evidence from satellites and seismic data we have reviewed suggest that an enormous mass of bedrock and glacier ice broke off a slope north of Langtang Lirung and slammed into the valley about 4,000 feet (1,200 meters) below – that’s a distance roughly three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. The landslide shook the earth hard enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 event on seismometers, the U.S. Geological Survey confirmed.

The result was a slurry of melting ice, rock and water that quickly flowed into the river.

We have a rough idea of how much ice fell, and it likely wouldn’t have been enough to trigger the magnitude of the flood that followed. One theory is that the rock and ice briefly dammed the valley, allowing water to back up in the river.

When that blockage broke, a wall of water rushed downstream – reaching towns, taking hundreds of lives and destroying infrastructure. Hundreds more people were stranded by the flood.

Second threat: The lake that formed, then burst

The disaster wasn’t finished when the first wall of water passed. Within a day, authorities warned that a new “barrier lake” estimated to hold a few million cubic meters of water had developed behind avalanche and flood debris where two rivers meet in Tibet, a region of China, before crossing into Nepal.

On Aug. 28, the barrier lake broke its bank and the river rose again. Helicopter search operations were briefly suspended while rescuers and residents on the lower banks scrambled to high ground. The immediate danger eased only when the barrier drained gradually rather than collapsing all at once.

Rescue personnel carry a person caught in the flash flood in Devghat, Nepal, on Aug. 26, 2026. Prakash Mathema/AFP via Getty Images

This is the crux of why these events are so dangerous: A temporary, debris-choked dam can form in minutes, hold for hours or days, and fail with little warning. An avalanche-dammed lake often appears and disappears too quickly for conventional monitoring to catch.

Risks are rising

We’re seeing disasters like this happen frequently.

In 2021, a similar rock and ice avalanche in India’s Uttarakhand state sent about 950 million cubic feet (27 million cubic meters) of rock and ice – roughly 80% rock, 20% ice – cascading down from Ronti Peak. It destroyed one hydropower plant, badly damaged another and killed or left missing about 200 people, many of them dam workers.

In 2025, roughly 335 million cubic feet (9.5 million cubic meters) of rock and ice fell from the Birch Glacier in the Swiss Alps, burying most of the village of Blatten; only advance monitoring and the evacuation of more than 300 residents kept the death toll to one.

The number of glacial lakes has also increased around the world, raising the risk of outburst floods. And more mountain slopes are now at risk of landslides than in the past.

In 2023, thawing permafrost led to a rock collapse into South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, India, generating a wave that burst through the moraine holding back the glacial lake. The outburst flood sent more than 13 billion gallons (50 million cubic meters) of water rushing down the mountain, damaging several dams, more than 25,000 buildings and more than 30 bridges.

Climate change is one major contributor to rising disaster risk.

The last 10 years have been the warmest on record globally, and that has accelerated snow and glacier melt.

Populations are growing, too, and these valleys are increasingly being used to generate hydropower. As countries build more infrastructure in these places, the hazard risk rises because more people and development sit in the flood’s path.

The valley where the latest disaster occurred held multiple hydropower plants – Nepal’s electricity authority said the flood knocked about a dozen major generation and transmission facilities offline. Bridges and a major border crossing, the Gyirong Port gateway between Nepal and China, were also destroyed. It became a catastrophe because of where the water, rock and mud landed.

Thawing permafrost, geology raise flood risk

Together with the neighboring Hindu Kush mountains, the rugged Himalayas that stretch across Asia contain one of the world’s largest volumes of ice. They’re sometimes called the “third pole” for that reason.

As temperatures have risen, their ice loss rates roughly doubled since 2000, according to studies from the Nepal-based International Center for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD.

And it isn’t only the glaciers that are melting. High mountain slopes are also held together by permafrost – ground that stays frozen year-round – with ice filling the cracks and joints in the rock like a natural cement. As that frozen ground warms and ice inside thaws, the cement weakens, and slopes that stood for thousands of years can lose their grip.

Meltwater from snow and ice seeps into cracks in the rock. Where it refreezes, it can pry those cracks wider. Where it stays liquid, it acts as a lubricant along the surfaces where rock and ice meet.

On a steep cliff, these water-filled fractures can sometimes be the difference between a face that holds and one that gives way all at once – sending millions of tons of rock and ice into the valley below in seconds.

Residents run through a mud-covered street, where the debris shows the flood reached well into the second flood of homes, on Aug. 26, 2026. Hundreds of people are missing on the Nepal-Tibet border after the flood swept away homes and cut off villages. Prabin Ranabhat/AFP via Getty Images

Not every thaw ends in disaster. But rising temperatures steadily load the dice: more slopes lose their frozen glue, more meltwater works its way into the cracks, and the odds of a catastrophic collapse rise year after year.

In the 2021 disaster in Uttarakhand, thawing likely contributed to the collapse of a large slab of rock and ice on the face of Ronti Peak.

Early indications in Nepal point to a similar story: a large mass of rock and ice detaching from a mountainside and falling, triggering the August 2026 flood. Comparing satellite images of the site from before and after, first posted by my colleague Dan Shugar, we have also noticed that a lot of snow had disappeared in the days preceding the flood. That snowmelt had to go somewhere – and it may have supplied the water that lubricated the rockfall.

How to lower the risk

From a risk standpoint, some areas of these mountains are extremely dangerous today.

To help protect people, early warning systems are crucial. When a flood starts, people living farther down the valley might have several minutes to get to safety before the water arrives – and minutes are enough to save lives.

Nepal has warning systems in place, and they have been credited with preventing casualties in the past. But the warning systems rely heavily on river-level gauges, which work far better for monsoon floods than for a wall of water moving tens of meters per second – and the flood itself likely destroyed the very gauges the warning systems depend on.

Building redundancy into the system would help, such as adding seismic sensors that detect a large mass movement the instant it happens, sirens and loudspeakers in valley-bottom settlements, radio and satellite-based cell broadcasts that don’t rely on a single tower that a flood can sweep away, and automatic alerts triggered when an avalanche and sudden water and sediment level in the river jumps.

Knowing the risks can also improve permit decisions for hydropower dams, roads and buildings in high-hazard corridors – and it can push monitoring beyond the familiar checklist of large glacial lakes to hanging glaciers, steep ice-and-rock slopes, permafrost, and the short-lived debris dams that can be just as deadly.

Regional cooperation is also important. When rivers cross borders or a transboundary glacial lake has potential to fail, the disaster doesn’t stop at the border. The water that devastated Nepal began on the Tibetan side, and the barrier lake that threatened a second surge sat right on the frontier.

title: China censors videos showing deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border - BBC

full_article:
Dramatic footage showing flash floods tearing through the main border crossing between Nepal and Tibet has been widely shared around the world.

But the footage has become almost impossible to find on China's heavily censored internet service, with only a single image broadcast by state media.

Hundreds of people are feared dead, and thousands remain missing as a major rescue operation continues into the weekend.

On Saturday, Chinese state media shared videos of rescue teams searching through mud and debris, but there has been little footage of the floods themselves, or accounts from survivors or anxious families.

Tibet remains a highly sensitive subject for China following its annexation in the 1950s. The region has long demanded greater autonomy and is one of the most strictly controlled regions in the country, with access for foreign media tightly restricted.

Read more on this story.

title: Pope Leo prays for victims of devastating Nepal floods - Vatican News
description: Pope Leo prays for victims of devastating Nepal floods  Vatican News
publisher.title: Vatican News
full_article:
Vatican News

Pope Leo XIV has expressed his deep sorrow over the loss of life and widespread devastation caused by flash floods in Nepal.

In a telegram sent on Thursday and signed by Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin, the Pope commended the souls of those who died “to the clemency of the Almighty” and offered his heartfelt condolences to the bereaved.

He also assured all those affected by the disaster of his spiritual closeness and prayed for the emergency personnel engaged in the ongoing search-and-rescue operations.

The telegram concluded with the Pope's prayers for God’s assistance and protection upon the people of Nepal.

Hundreds dead or missing

Over 350 people have died in Nepal, while more than 900 remain unaccounted for after a devastating torrent of water, mud and debris swept through communities near the country’s northern border with China. Unfortunately, the death toll is expected to rise as bodies are recovered from under the debris.

Hundreds more are missing in neighbouring Tibet, bringing the total number of people unaccounted for across the affected region to almost 1,500.

The disaster is believed to have been triggered by the collapse of part of a Himalayan glacier, which sent a sudden surge into a river system along the Nepal-China border. Scientists said the force of the collapse was so great that the resulting tremors were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

Entire settlements were inundated, while roads, bridges, power installations and other essential infrastructure were destroyed or severely damaged. The floods also struck a major border crossing, cutting off transport and trade routes.

Many of those missing are foreign visitors who had travelled to the region on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar, sites considered sacred by Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of the Bon religion.

Rescue operations continue

Thousands of soldiers, police officers and emergency workers have been deployed across the affected areas. Helicopters are being used to reach isolated communities, evacuate survivors and deliver food, medical supplies and other forms of emergency assistance.

Operations are being complicated by damaged roads, difficult mountainous terrain and the continuing danger of landslides and further flooding.

International aid has begun to arrive, with neighbouring countries, the United Nations and humanitarian organisations offering personnel, supplies and financial assistance.

The tragedy has also renewed concerns about the growing threat posed by glacial instability in the Himalayas, where rising temperatures are accelerating the melting and retreat of glaciers.

title: Daughter traces mother and aunt’s last known location in Nepal through TikTok video - The Guardian
description: Daughter traces mother and aunt’s last known location in Nepal through TikTok video  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
The daughter of a woman missing in Nepal has told how she traced her mother’s location through a TikTok video posted hours before the devastating flash flood hit.

The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 675 people, while more than 3,000 remain missing.

Among the missing are 33 British nationals, including a 13-year-old, NHS workers and a priest. A team from the UK will arrive in the Nepali capital, Kathmandu, on Saturday.

Tulshi Patel’s mother, Hemangini Jitendra Patel, and her aunt, Hema Sunil Amin, set off on a pilgrimage in which they had planned to travel into Tibet, but the pair have not been contactable since the flash floods hit.

In an interview with LBC’s Matt Frei, Patel said the two women had been talking about the trip since the start of the year and the journey had been “on their bucket list”.

She said she had last spoken to her mother and aunt on Monday, had received a photo of them on Tuesday, and their last known location had come from a GPS signal from the tour group at a place called Friendship Bridge at the Nepal-China border.

View image in fullscreen The Chinese immigration centre on the Tibet border. The green Friendship Bridge which crosses the river between Tibet and Nepal was swept away in the floods. Photograph: Armand Terruli/Guardian Community

Patel, a pharmacist from Milton Keynes, said: “We did our own deep-dive research and we found a TikTok video that verified and showed my mum and auntie and three other people from the tour at the border waiting to cross, I guess, that the local Nepali tour guide had made.”

Of the video, Patel said: “It was Wednesday morning, just before 6am, Nepal time.

“They were supposed to have crossed the border on Tuesday, but I guess due to weather conditions, or whichever it was, they got delayed and unfortunately crossed over on Wednesday.”

The flood is believed to have occurred after a magnitude 5.2 seismic event near the border between Nepal and China on Wednesday at 8.37am local time, according to the US Geological Survey.

Patel said her mother and aunt had been in good health and had prepared well for the trip. “They’d gone on walks regularly, they were looking forward to it. This is all they wanted,” she said.

“Their positive viewpoints, health, mental health was great and they were very strong and positive about everything.

“This was something that they were both looking forward to. They’d been talking about this from the beginning of the year. It was something that was on their bucket list that they really wanted to do.”

Neetu Goyal Tiwari. Photograph: Facebook

Patel said she had messaged the two women “in the hopes that maybe we’ll see a tick to say they’ve seen it or read it” and had attempted to contact the tour guide. “We’ve messaged the tour guide in case he has a signal because he’ll have a local Sim as well.

“Every day we’re calling via WhatsApp … We’ve not given up, but, from our end, all we can do is research, but we just need kind of eyes and ears there from our side to basically get them out. Get all of them out and safe.”

Patel said the family had considered travelling to Nepal to join search efforts but had decided against this as they did not know how close they could get to the region in order to help.

View image in fullscreen Leena Bector. Photograph: Facebook

Some of those missing were visiting Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists. Neetu Goyal Tiwari, 51, was on her “dream” trip to complete a pilgrimage when the flash floods hit.

The family have been desperately phoning contacts in Nepal in an attempt to find her, though they increasingly believe her to still be in China. As many of the family members are based in India, it is difficult for them to obtain visas to search for her. Her brother, Naresh Goyal, said Neetu’s husband and daughter remained in the UK for now.

“We’re not sure what the next second holds and what we should do from our end, because we’re trying to reach everyone we can,” he said. “She was a very fun-loving woman [and] really had a great heart. I really hope she comes back soon.”

Other families of those missing have travelled to the affected region from the UK. Leena Bector, 53, from Slough, was among 27 travellers who are unaccounted for.

Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told the Times he was booking the next flight to Kathmandu after the Home Office had failed to confirm whether Leena was on its missing persons list.

He said: “Even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there. She must be in trauma.”

title: Suburban family devastated after woman goes missing in Nepal amid flash floods: 'She's somewhere' - Chicago Sun-Times
description: Suburban family devastated after woman goes missing in Nepal amid flash floods: 'She's somewhere'  Chicago Sun-Times
publisher.title: Chicago Sun-Times
full_article:
A suburban family is clinging to hope as they search for their loved one who went missing in the catastrophic flash floods in Nepal on Wednesday.

Poonam Dilipkumar Thakkar, 42, left her home in Bartlett for Nepal last Thursday for a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity” to visit Mount Kailash.

She traveled to the region as part of a religious pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which Hindus believe is the home of the god Shiva.

Thakkar checked in with her family from Hotel Kailash in Timure where she was staying Wednesday morning.

But the hotel is no longer standing, her family said.

Shortly after Thakkar’s call home, massive flash floods swept through the border region between Nepal and China, wiping out communities and leaving thousands of people missing.

Her family hasn’t heard from her since.

Experts said the flash floods were caused by a glacial collapse. Nepal’s disaster agency said Saturday, the death toll had climbed to 669 with 2,426 people still missing . More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far.

“We’re still trying to hold on to hope that she will be found, but it’s very difficult seeing the amount of destruction that has happened in that region,” said Esha Sachdev, Thakkar’s niece.

Poonam Dilipkumar Thakkar with her family Provided

Sachdev said the family has tried to reach government agencies and community groups who may be able to help search for Thakkar, who is a U.S. and Canadian citizen, but haven’t gotten many answers.

The U.S. Embassy in Nepal did not respond to a request for comment.

Nepali authorities said search-and-rescue teams continue to search for people in the affected areas.

Her family said Thakkar has always loved traveling and visiting new places. Her trip to Nepal was one she had wanted to take for years, and she traveled with an excursion group.

The travel agency said everyone in the group remains missing, including the guides.

“We have to depend on the government and abide by the protocol currently established,” said Sanket Pandey, managing director at Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company. “We’re also keeping an eye on any new lists that get released of the rescued.”

Sanday said the company has an operational headquarters in Nepal, where the CEO and team leaders are in the region “overseeing all possible aid.”

Poonam Dilipkumar Thakkar (center) with her sisters Provided

But for their family, waiting for answers is no longer enough, Sachdev said. That’s why her mother, Bhumika Sachdev, Thakkar’s oldest sister, plans to fly to Nepal on Sunday.

The family said they fear rescue teams will stop searching for survivors in the area where Thakkar went missing.

When she arrives, Bhumika Sachdev, 49, said she hopes to get in contact with organizations who will help her search for her sister.

“It’s not just us,” she said. “There are other families who are suffering like this too, who cannot find the whereabouts of their friends and family. So it’s just very disheartening right now.”

But the family said they won’t give up until she is found.

“We have hope that she will be found,” her sister said. “She’s somewhere.”

title: California mom makes miracle escape during Nepal flood disaster - New York Post
description: California mom makes miracle escape during Nepal flood disaster  New York Post
publisher.title: New York Post
full_article:
A California mother who made her dream trip to Nepal has revealed her horror at being caught up in a catastrophic flash flood that killed more than 600 people.

Anjana Raja and her husband Pattabiraman Venkatesan, from the Bay Area, were among the American survivors of Wednesday’s terrifying disaster.

4 A couple from the San Francisco Bay Area, who were on a pilgrimage, survived a glacier flood in Nepal. CBS NEWS

4 Houses are seen in ruins in Bidur, Nepal, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026, YONHAP/EPA/Shutterstock

She said she was certain she was going to die when she saw a mountain of water surging towards them near the country’s border with China.

A massive torrent up to 160ft high was caught on video as it swept over the district of Rasuwa following a huge glacial rock and ice collapse that was so powerful it registered a magnitude of 5.2.

As many as 682 people are known to have been killed with thousands more still missing, including about 90 Americans. No one from the US has been confirmed dead.

Raja told how she was sitting on a bus when the driver and front passengers suddenly fled and left them when the landslide and water swept in.

She told CBS News: “I knew I was going to die. I knew I was going to die.” That thought popped up, she said, when they saw a mountain of water coming toward them.

She continued to ABC News: “It was water mixed with the mud that was a good 50 to 60 feet high. It stood like a serpent right there staring at us. Like a cobra’s head staring at you.”

She said she immediately grabbed her bag and her husband by the collar to rush out. She continued: “I just said, ‘leave the bus right away or we’re gonna die.'”

The couple and other bus passengers ran to a nearby camp and ascended to higher ground as the water flooded the streets.

As they climbed frantically, Raja remembered seeing the water level rising toward them, which made her think it was over for them.

4 Indian pilgrims, who were stranded in Saga in China’s Tibet during their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, are greeted by family members upon their arrival from Kathmandu at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport in Mumbai, India, on Saturday, August 29, 2026. The pilgrims had been stranded following deadly flash floods and mudslides. REUTERS

Fortunately, the water never reached their level.

“It just came like a roar, it sucked a bunch of buses, SUVs, people, the basecamp, everything — took it in, turned it, turned it all upside down and dumped it into the ground,” Raja said of the water’s power.

She had been in Nepal to do a spiritual pilgrimage to Mount Kailash. The peak is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and believers of the pre-Buddhist Bon religion.

Instead, she ended up spending the night in a goat shed with other survivors before being airlifted by rescuers the next day. The couple made contact with their daughter, a physician in California.

Venkatesan, her husband, described their survival as a “miracle” and strengthened his appreciation of life. They said they still plan on one day finishing their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.

The flooding is believed to have been triggered when the lower part of a glacier broke off and fell from a height of around 17,000 feet, smashing into a valley floor, creating what is known as an ice avalanche.

It was not clear what caused the glacier to collapse, but the powerful torrent of water and debris it caused swept away homes, roads and businesses in Nepal.

title: His family’s Baltimore business sent travelers to Nepal. Then the floods hit. - The Baltimore Banner
description: His family’s Baltimore business sent travelers to Nepal. Then the floods hit.  The Baltimore Banner
publisher.title: The Baltimore Banner
full_article:
On early Wednesday morning, a tour group operated by Baltimore-based company Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Co. was preparing to enter Tibet and travel to Mount Kailash, a revered site among Hindus, Jains and Buddhists.

The group, which included 40 travelers and seven guides, was looking forward to following the footsteps of millions of other pilgrims by touching the holy water of Lake Manasarovar and circling the sacred mountain clockwise, said the company’s managing director Sanket Pandey.

But then, disaster struck.

Catastrophic flash floods swept through the area of Nepal where the group was staying, destroying roads and buildings and killing hundreds. The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose on Saturday to 676 dead and nearly 3,000 people missing, according to the Associated Press.

Advertise with us

That includes all 47 traveling with Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel, whose group featured tourists from U.S., Canada and Australia.

The last time anyone from the company heard from the group was during a check-in Wednesday morning as they finished breakfast, Sanket said. The group, which had divided up to stay in two different hotels, was planning to meet before crossing into Tibet.

Read More Baltimore-based tour company’s group among missing in Nepal-China floods Aug 28, 2026

Since the flash floods, Sanket has spent his days fielding calls from family members of the missing and sharing news coming from Nepal, from where his father and the company’s CEO, Sagar Pandey, has been coordinating efforts.

Sanket said in an interview Saturday that he is “just trying to keep every bit of sanity and provide any bit of comfort to the families.”

Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel is limited in what it can do because access to the disaster zone is still limited, Sanket said.

Advertise with us

Some family members are trying to get access to the last known GPS coordinates of the travelers through their wearable devices or phones, he said. But many technology companies only release information to law enforcement, which require relatives to first file missing persons reports.

“We’re trying to do everything we can to find people alive,” Sanket said.

Sanket also has a family member, who works as a guide for the company, among the missing.

Sanket’s father, Sagar, founded Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel in Nepal in 1992. Sagar got the idea from a trek he completed while in field training as a college student studying geology, according to Sanket.

Inspired by the mountainous landscape and people he met along the way, Sagar dropped out of school so he could help other people experience what he did.

Advertise with us

The company started with offering trips to Nepal and has branched out to Tanzania and Peru, Sanket said. It specializes in cultural tours and adventure travel.

Sanket, after graduating from Towson University with a degree in finance, helped his family establish their business in Baltimore in 2019.

It made sense to expand to the U.S. because most of their clientele was coming from North America, he said.

Sanket said the company never imagined something so catastrophic would happen.

“I do believe in miracles,” he said, “but every passing it probably just dwindles.”

Anil Goel, an avid hiker from Virginia, went missing when the floods struck during his multi-day hiking trip to Mount Kailash in Tibet near the Nepal-China border.

Goel’s hiking group was last known to have received their departure stamps on their passports to leave Nepal around 8:35 a.m., followed by some WhatsApp exchanges around the same time, his son, Anurag Goel, told CNN’s Victor Blackwell on “First of All” today.

Roughly 45 minutes later, the floods struck.

“It’s been really challenging, just dealing with the uncertainty and dealing with lack of communication and the sheer vastness of the disaster,” Anurag Goel said.

He is working with various local authorities and other affected families to aid in the search efforts.

“What’s been really helpful is communicating with other families that are also impacted, that are missing loved ones in the region, and understanding what these other families are doing, resources they’re utilizing,” Goel said. “But it’s impossible to know how we can go about identifying people that are being recovered, rescued from that region. That’s been a real challenge.”

Despite the challenges, he remains hopeful and encourages others to support the search.

Anurag Goel is also finding comfort in his father’s YouTube videos, posted from the trip, which highlight the beauty of the region. “I do try to … look at those videos and get more perspective on why it’s such a beloved area for many,” he told CNN.

Rescuers in Nepal and China on Saturday battled to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing entire villages.

Figures from both countries put the number of missing close to 3,000, with 682 bodies recovered – and reports of some dead possibly swept downstream as far away as India.

In a breakthrough late Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.

More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.

The US Geological Survey said a glacial collapse was behind the deadly torrent on Wednesday at the Nepal-Tibet border.

While the exact cause of the collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

"The sudden glacial collapse and flash flood is a devastating reminder of how fragile these mountain environments can be", UN climate chief Simon Steill said in a statement.

"We also know a warming climate, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making tragedies like this one, and so many others around the world, much more likely, frequent and severe, with vulnerable communities often hardest hit," he added.

'Nothing left'

Survivors face an agonising wait to learn the fate of missing relatives, and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.

"All the settlements near the river were swept away," Buddhi Ram Dangol said in Nepal's Nuwakot district. "There is nothing left."

At an army base serving as a key rescue hub in Bidur, relatives crowded around lists of rescued people pasted on a wall.

"I have come here looking for my son," said Kalka Sharda, scanning the list in desperation. "He was a labourer at the hydropower plant, but I can't find his name, and the authorities are not saying anything."

In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal's disaster authority listed 933 hydropower workers among the missing, along with 517 foreigners, including trekkers and Hindu pilgrims to Tibet's sacred Mount Kailash.

The Isha Foundation, led by Indian guru Sadhguru, said in an Instagram post on Saturday that 80 members had been on a group trip in the area.

The group was at the hard-hit Chinese border port of Gyirong, which has been "completely washed away", the post said.

"At this time, there seems to be no encouraging indications of survivors at the immigration office area."

'Enormous' trauma

Nepal's reconstruction bill could run into "billions of dollars", Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said Saturday.

"The urgency is on rescue and saving lives as much as we can," he said, appealing for specialised assistance, including heavy-lift drones and technology to help locate people who are trapped.

He also called for forensic testing kits to identify bodies and freezer units to store them, saying bodies that have been in water could decompose at a faster rate.

Fears of further flooding have compounded the search for the missing.

The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes, and one of these formations has become a risk of further floods.

The Chinese and Nepalese foreign ministers spoke Saturday and discussed sharing satellite and hydrological data, both sides said.

In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, rescue operations were temporarily paused at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of more flooding from a newly formed lake.

But state broadcaster CCTV said late Saturday that the lake was "discharging naturally" and had been "essentially drained", citing China's ministry of water resources.

A total of 2,141 rescuers were near the Gyirong site, the Xinhua state news agency reported, including more than 500 in the worst-hit area.

Pilgrimage route

Nepal reported a death toll of 675 people on Saturday.

There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in the country.

Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, seven people died and 554 remain missing, Xinhua state news agency said on Saturday.

Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.

In India, officials said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.

Hope was fading for some still waiting desperately for news.

Kalka Sharda, in Bidur, was searching lists of rescued for his 18-year-old son Vinod Sharda, a hydropower plant labourer.

"I don't think there is any hope left," he said.

"Because, if he was alive, he would have found a way to get in touch."
